reason: The sources contain 20 highly verified claims across multiple sites, detailing a tragic, historic space disaster.
story: In June 1971, three Soviet cosmonauts—Georgy Dobrovolsky, Vladislav Volkov, and Viktor Patsayev—launched aboard Soyuz 11. They successfully boarded Salyut 1, the world’s first space station, setting new space endurance records over three weeks. But their mission was doomed before it even launched; the original prime crew had been grounded just days prior due to a suspected tuberculosis diagnosis. When the replacement crew prepared to return to Earth, disaster struck. As their capsule separated from the service module at high altitude, the explosive separation charges accidentally jarred open a breathing ventilation valve. Crucially, the cosmonauts were not wearing pressure suits. The capsule's air quickly vented into the vacuum of space, suffocating the crew in less than a minute. Recovery teams opened the landed, undamaged capsule to find all three men dead in their seats. Today, they remain the only humans to have ever died in space.
angle: The crew of Soyuz 11 are the only humans to have ever died in space, suffocated when a faulty valve vented all their air into the vacuum of space because they weren't wearing spacesuits.

claims.claim: Soyuz 11 launched on June 6, 1971.
The crew consisted of Georgy Dobrovolsky, Vladislav Volkov, and Viktor Patsayev.
Soyuz 11 docked with Salyut 1, which was the world's first space station.
The original prime crew was replaced by their backups because Valery Kubasov was suspected of having tuberculosis.
The Soyuz 11 crew set a space endurance record during their mission.
The mission ended in tragedy when the spacecraft's capsule depressurized prior to atmospheric re-entry.
The depressurization was caused by a breathing ventilation/equalization valve that was jarred open during module separation.
The cosmonauts were not wearing pressurized suits during the re-entry.
All three cosmonauts died of asphyxiation/suffocation.
The capsule made an automatic landing in Kazakhstan.
Recovery forces opened the hatch to find the three crew members dead in their seats.
The deceased cosmonauts had blue splotches on their faces and blood trickling from their noses and ears.
The three cosmonauts of Soyuz 11 are the only humans to have died in space.
The crew was given a state funeral and buried in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis.
US President Richard Nixon issued a statement expressing deepest sympathy to the Soviet people.
American astronaut Thomas Stafford represented the US at the funeral and served as one of the pallbearers.
Following the accident, the Soyuz spacecraft was redesigned so that crews would wear pressure suits during launch and landing.
Craters on the Moon were named after Dobrovolsky, Volkov, and Patsayev.
The crew's names were included on the Fallen Astronaut commemorative plaque left on the Moon.
A group of hills on Pluto was named Soyuz Colles to honor the crew.

disputed: The exact duration of the mission is disputed, with some sources stating 22 days and others stating 24 days; a script should use general terms like 'over three weeks'.
The exact altitude at which the valve opened varies between 80, 100, and 104 miles; a script should refer to it generally as 'high altitude' or 'prior to re-entry'.
The exact date of death is given as June 29 or June 30 due to timezone differences; a script should refer to it as late June 1971.

The exact physiological cause of death is stated by one early source as a rise in blood pressure, while others state asphyxiation due to exposure to vacuum; a script should focus on the consensus of asphyxiation and decompression effects.
